case_analysis.focal_point: Whether requests for reimbursement submitted in the FCC’s E-rate program are “claims” under the False Claims Act even though the money comes from the Universal Service Fund (funded by private carrier contributions and administered by a program administrator) rather than directly from the U.S. Treasury.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3729 (especially § 3729(b)(2)’s definition of “claim” as amended by FERA), as applied to the E-rate program created under 47 U.S.C. § 254 and implemented by FCC regulations.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Wisconsin Bell argues that E-rate reimbursement submissions are not FCA “claims” because the E-rate program pays from the Universal Service Fund—funded by mandatory carrier contributions and disbursed through a non-federal administrator—so the reimbursement request is not a request for “money or property” provided by, or to be reimbursed by, the federal government within § 3729(b)(2). Petitioner (and supporting amici) emphasize that Congress drafted the FCA to protect the federal fisc and that treating E-rate paperwork as FCA claims would improperly extend FCA liability to transactions involving non-treasury funds and private or quasi-private intermediaries, creating expansive and uncertain exposure for regulated industries participating in complex federal programs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Heath (the relator) contends that E-rate reimbursement submissions are FCA “claims” because the program is federally created and federally supervised (FCC-directed), the funds exist only by force of federal law and are collected to serve a federal statutory purpose, and the government effectively controls how the money is raised and disbursed. On that view, E-rate payments are sufficiently “governmental” for § 3729(b)(2) because the requests seek payment under a federal program and involve money used to advance federal objectives; allowing FCA coverage is necessary to deter and remedy fraud in a large, federally mandated subsidy system.
key_precedents: United States ex rel. Shupe v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 759 F.3d 379 (5th Cir. 2014)
Universal Health Services, Inc. v. United States ex rel. Escobar, 579 U.S. 176 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that the Universal Service Fund is privately sourced and never enters the Treasury, so an E-rate reimbursement request looks unlike the paradigmatic FCA “claim” on federal money; but FERA’s amended definition squarely anticipates that objection by covering demands made to an “other recipient” to advance a Government program “whether or not the United States has title to the money,” § 3729(b)(2)(A). Justice Gorsuch’s textual point that importing a Treasury-only limitation would add words Congress did not enact reinforces my view that the custody of funds in USAC is not dispositive, particularly given the federally compelled and FCC-directed scheme under 47 U.S.C. § 254. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Marcus v. Hess usefully underscores that intermediaries and “bookkeeping devices” cannot be used to evade an anti-fraud statute aimed at federally directed payment programs. Consistent with institutional minimalism, I would affirm narrowly under § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) on these specific facts—pervasive federal control and a statutorily mandated funding stream—without opining on more marginal quasi-public or mixed-private arrangements, leaving Escobar’s materiality and scienter to do their work in cabining overbreadth.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the “no Treasury dollars/no federal title” argument, but the text Congress enacted in FERA directly rejects making custody or title dispositive: § 3729(b)(2)(A) reaches demands to an “other recipient” for money used to advance a Government program “whether or not the United States has title.” Justice Gorsuch’s warning that a Treasury-only gloss on “provides” would add a limitation Congress did not write is decisive under a textualist approach, especially given § 254’s federally compelled collection and federally directed disbursement structure. The conduit-focused reasoning in cases like Shupe is therefore at best a pre-FERA artifact and cannot override the amended statutory definition’s ordinary public meaning. I agree with the Chief Justice that we can affirm narrowly on § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) and this program’s pervasive federal control, without pronouncing on more marginal quasi-private funds.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the Shupe-style contention that, because E-rate funds never enter the Treasury and are privately sourced, a reimbursement request is not a “claim” on the United States. But as the Chief Justice notes, FERA’s amended definition squarely reaches demands made to an “other recipient” for money used “to advance a Government program or interest” and does so “whether or not the United States has title to the money,” which leaves little room for a Treasury-only limitation. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Marcus v. Hess further reinforces that we should not allow an intermediary or routing choice (USAC) to become a “bookkeeping device” that defeats Congress’s anti-fraud design in a federally compelled, federally directed program under 47 U.S.C. § 254. I would adopt Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower, text-bound rationale limited to these facts and § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii), which also mitigates legitimate overbreadth concerns without rewriting the statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument—that E-rate disbursements aren’t “Government money” because they never enter the Treasury and derive from carrier contributions—can’t overcome FERA’s amended text, which covers demands advancing a federal program “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” Justice Gorsuch’s point that a Treasury-only reading of “provide” would add a limitation Congress did not write fits my own understanding that the Government can “provide” funds by mandating their collection and dictating their use through pervasive FCC control under § 254. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marcus v. Hess is also persuasive in answering the conduit/formalities objection: routing through USAC is the kind of bookkeeping device Congress meant to be irrelevant when federal law creates and directs the payment stream. Pragmatically, excluding E-rate from the FCA would create an enforcement gap that predictably harms schools and libraries, while Escobar’s materiality and the FCA’s scienter requirements remain real constraints against overreach.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the “no Treasury dollars, no FCA claim” theory, but the FERA amendment squarely rejects making federal title or Treasury custody dispositive by covering demands to an “other recipient” for money used to advance a Government program “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” Justice Gorsuch’s ordinary-meaning argument about “provides” is persuasive under a pragmatic textualist approach: the Government can “provide” funds by legally compelling their collection and dictating their use within a federally created program, even if an intermediary like USAC holds and disburses the money. Justice Thomas’s Marcus v. Hess “bookkeeping device” point reinforces that Congress aimed at fraud against federally directed payment streams and would not have wanted liability to turn on routing mechanics. I agree with the Chief Justice’s call for a narrow holding under § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) tied to the pervasive federal control of E-rate, leaving harder boundary cases for another day while relying on Escobar’s materiality and the FCA’s scienter to prevent overbreadth.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the “no Treasury dollars, no FCA claim” theory, but the 2009 FERA text forecloses that move by covering demands that advance a Government program “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” Justice Barrett’s ordinary-meaning account of “provide” as “make available” fits this program: federal law compels the fund’s collection and dictates its use, so the Government “provides” the money in the relevant statutory sense even if USAC holds and disburses it. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marcus v. Hess further confirms that FCA coverage cannot turn on “bookkeeping devices” like routing through intermediaries, and I agree with the Chief Justice’s suggestion to resolve this case narrowly under § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) without announcing outer limits for other mixed funds. Nothing raised in conference shows a textual basis to insert a Treasury-only limitation that Congress did not enact.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that USF monies are not Treasury funds and are disbursed by USAC, but the post-FERA definition expressly removes federal title/custody as dispositive by covering demands advancing a Government program “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow path is the right institutional approach: on these facts, E-rate reimbursement requests fall within § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) because § 254 creates the program and the FCC mandates collection and directs disbursement, without our needing to announce a broad rule for every quasi-public fund. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marcus v. Hess strengthens the response to the “intermediary/bookkeeping” objection by confirming that routing payments through a non-Treasury administrator does not defeat FCA coverage when federal law creates and controls the payment stream. Overbreadth concerns are better handled, as Roberts and others note, through Escobar’s materiality and the FCA’s scienter requirements rather than by importing an extra-textual Treasury-only limitation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that the Government does not “provide” E-rate funds because they never enter the Treasury and remain outside federal title—runs into the enacted text of § 3729(b)(2)(A), which expressly applies “whether or not the United States has title to the money” and thus makes custody/title an insufficient limitation. Justice Gorsuch’s ordinary-meaning point is decisive under a textualist approach: to “provide” can mean to furnish or make available, and the Government does so here by compelling collection and directing disbursement under § 254 and FCC regulation, even if USAC writes the checks. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marcus v. Hess strengthens the conclusion that routing payments through an intermediary is a “bookkeeping” detail that cannot defeat FCA coverage when Congress has defined “claim” to reach demands advancing a Government program. I agree with the Chief Justice’s proposal to affirm on the narrower ground that these facts fall within § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii), leaving harder questions about more weakly federalized funds for another day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Treasury-title theory—that FCA coverage should stop when dollars never enter the Treasury and are held by USAC—but FERA’s amended definition expressly rejects making federal title dispositive by reaching demands to an “other recipient” for money used to advance a Government program “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” Justice Gorsuch’s ordinary-meaning focus on “provide” (as making funds available through compelled collection and federally directed disbursement) answers the textual hook, while Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marcus v. Hess persuasively shows why intermediaries and bookkeeping devices cannot be allowed to create an enforcement gap in a federally created program. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we should keep the holding narrow—grounded in § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) and the pervasive federal control under § 254—leaving harder boundary cases for another day, with Escobar’s materiality and the FCA’s scienter requirements serving as practical constraints against overbreadth. Nothing raised in conference genuinely undermines that these reimbursement submissions are “claims” under the post-FERA statutory text on these facts.

John Roberts.reasoning: FERA’s amended definition of “claim” reaches demands made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” where the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and it applies “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). The E-rate program is a federally created and FCC-directed subsidy mechanism under 47 U.S.C. § 254; the fact that disbursements run through the Universal Service Fund and an administrator does not, on the statutory text Congress chose, take reimbursement requests outside the FCA’s definition. A narrow, institutionally modest ruling can affirm on the ground that E-rate submissions qualify at least under § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) because they seek payment to advance a federal program under pervasive federal direction, without deciding the outer bounds for all quasi-public funds. Escobar reinforces a restrained approach to FCA scope and materiality in policing fraud in federal programs while adhering closely to statutory text and settled interpretive principles.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the text of the FCA as amended by FERA, a “claim” includes a request for money made to a contractor or other recipient where the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). The E-rate program is a federally created and federally directed subsidy under 47 U.S.C. § 254, and reimbursement requests seek payment from funds collected and disbursed only by force of federal law to advance that federal program, even if administered by USAC rather than paid directly from the Treasury. Marcus v. Hess instructs that FCA coverage does not turn on “bookkeeping devices” or the use of intermediaries when federal program funds are the object of the fraud, 317 U.S. 537, 544 (1943). On the statute’s original public meaning as revised by Congress in FERA’s text, routing funds through a non-federal administrator does not remove such demands from the FCA’s definition of “claim.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FERA’s amended definition of “claim” in 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2) reaches demands for money made to a recipient when the money is “spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and E-rate disbursements—though routed through USAC and sourced from mandatory carrier contributions—exist only by force of federal law and are tightly directed by the FCC under 47 U.S.C. § 254. Textually, the program’s structure makes the reimbursement request one for funds used to advance a federal program, and the practical consequence of excluding such submissions would be to create a substantial fraud-enforcement gap in a large federally mandated subsidy system. While Shupe v. Cisco Systems, 759 F.3d 379 (5th Cir. 2014), treated the absence of Treasury dollars as dispositive, that approach gives undue weight to the payment conduit and underreads Congress’s post-2009 expansion aimed at covering fraud in federally supervised programs financed outside the Treasury. Consistent with Escobar’s emphasis that the FCA targets material misrepresentations that affect payment decisions, E-rate reimbursement submissions should be treated as FCA “claims” where falsehoods are material to the program administrator’s disbursement determinations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FERA’s 2009 amendment defines a “claim” to include demands made to a “contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the requested money “is to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and does so “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). The E-rate program exists only by federal statute (47 U.S.C. § 254) and is federally supervised by the FCC, so reimbursement submissions seek payment from a federally mandated fund that advances a federal program—even if administered through a non-Treasury intermediary—bringing them within the text Congress chose. Reading the FCA to exclude such federally directed subsidy payments would undermine deterrence and remedies for fraud in programs designed to expand access for schools and libraries, while the statute’s materiality limits (as emphasized in Escobar) guard against overbroad liability for minor regulatory missteps.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FERA’s amended definition of “claim” in 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2) reaches requests for money presented to a contractor/administrator (USAC) when the money is “to advance a Government program or interest” and the Government “provides or has provided any portion” of it or will reimburse it; E-rate fits that text because the Fund exists only by federal mandate under 47 U.S.C. § 254 and is disbursed under FCC supervision to serve a federal objective. The fact that contributions are collected from private carriers and held/disbursed through a non-Treasury intermediary does not defeat FCA coverage where federal law compels the funding stream and federal regulators control the program’s purposes and payments, making the requests functionally demands on a federal program. That reading is also the most workable: it avoids turning FCA coverage on formalities about account custody while still hewing to the statute’s post-FERA focus on fraud that drains federally directed program funds. Consistent with Escobar, recognizing these submissions as “claims” preserves FCA’s central deterrent role in large federal payment programs without expanding liability beyond the statute’s text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FERA’s amended definition reaches a request for money made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” so long as the money is to be spent “on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest” and the Government “provides or has provided any portion of the money or property requested.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). Under the ordinary meaning of “provide,” Congress can “furnish” money not only by paying from the Treasury but also by mandating exactions for a federal statutory program and directing their collection and disbursement through an administrator under federal control; the E-rate fund exists and is disbursed only by force of federal law and to advance § 254’s federal objectives. Reading “provide” to require a Treasury transfer would add words Congress did not choose, narrowing § 3729(b)(2) despite FERA’s evident intent to capture frauds involving intermediaries and nontraditional payment mechanisms. Escobar confirms the FCA’s focus on material fraud in federal programs, and this construction fits that textual design without resorting to agency deference.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FERA-amended text defines a “claim” to include requests presented to a “contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the money is “to be spent … on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and the E-rate reimbursements are disbursed pursuant to a federally created, FCC-controlled subsidy program under 47 U.S.C. § 254 and implementing regulations. Even though the Universal Service Fund is financed by carrier contributions and administered through USAC, the payments are made only because federal law mandates the funding mechanism and tightly specifies who pays, who receives, and for what purposes—making the reimbursement request functionally a request for program funds “to advance a Government program.” This reading is consistent with Escobar’s emphasis on adhering to the FCA’s statutory text and ensuring a workable anti-fraud regime for major federal programs, while distinguishing cases like Costner where the fund was privately created and not under comparable federal control. Limiting FCA coverage here would invite an easily exploitable loophole for federal programs structured through intermediaries, undermining Congress’s post-FERA expansion of the definition of “claim.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The post-FERA text of the FCA defines a “claim” to include demands made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the money is “to be spent … to advance a Government program or interest” and the “Government … provides or has provided any portion of the money.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). Reading “provides” in its ordinary sense (“makes available”), the United States “provides” the E-rate funds because federal law compels their collection, the FCC controls their disposition under 47 U.S.C. § 254, and USAC disburses them only as an administrator of a federal program—so reimbursement requests are demands for money made available under governmental direction even if not drawn from the Treasury. Congress enacted FERA against the backdrop of Totten and Allison Engine and amended the definition precisely to reach claims routed through intermediaries and to protect federal programs beyond direct Treasury payments, so methodological consistency and text favor coverage here. Escobar underscores that the FCA reaches fraud in federally supervised payment schemes, and nothing in § 3729(b)(2) limits “provided by” to Treasury appropriations or federal title.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under FERA’s amended definition, a “claim” includes any request for money presented to the United States or its “agent,” so long as the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” “whether or not the United States has title to the money.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). The E-rate reimbursements are disbursed under a federally created and FCC-supervised statutory scheme (47 U.S.C. § 254), and the Universal Service Fund exists only because federal law mandates its collection and prescribes its use; that functional federal control makes the requested funds “provided” for and used to advance a federal program even if not paid from the Treasury. Reading § 3729(b)(2) to exclude such federally compelled, federally directed subsidy payments would narrow the statute by inserting a “Treasury-only” limitation Congress expressly rejected in 2009, and it would undermine the FCA’s practical anti-fraud purpose in large federal programs. While Escobar addresses materiality rather than the definition of “claim,” its insistence on rigorous, program-sensitive enforcement supports applying the FCA here while policing overbreadth through materiality and scienter requirements.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether reimbursement requests made within the FCC’s E-rate program—processed through the Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC) and funded by industry contributions—qualify as “claims” under the False Claims Act because they involve federal money or property.
case_analysis.legal_provision: False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729 et seq.), particularly the definition of “claim” in 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2) (and its requirements relating to presentment to the United States, or to a contractor/grantee/other recipient when U.S. funds are involved or the United States provides or reimburses money).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Wisconsin Bell argues that E-rate reimbursement requests are not FCA “claims” because they are not demands for money or property of the United States: E-rate support is paid from the Universal Service Fund, which is financed by mandatory contributions from telecommunications providers and administered by USAC (a non-federal entity), so the money requested is not “provided” by the federal government and is not U.S. Treasury money; treating such requests as FCA claims would improperly expand the FCA beyond its statutory text and historical focus on protecting federal fisc and would expose regulated entities to FCA liability for disputes arising within a complex regulatory subsidy program.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Heath (relator for the United States) argues that E-rate reimbursement requests are FCA “claims” because the E-rate program is a federal program created and overseen by the FCC, the Universal Service Fund is federally mandated and federally controlled (even if collected from private contributors and administered by USAC), and the requests are functionally demands for payment under a federal program; accordingly, false submissions that induce E-rate disbursements are the type of fraud the FCA reaches, and excluding E-rate requests would create a significant enforcement gap for misconduct affecting a federal program and funds directed by federal law.
key_precedents: United States ex rel. Shupe v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 759 F.3d 379 (5th Cir. 2014)
United States ex rel. Heath v. Wisconsin Bell, Inc. (district court proceedings referenced in the materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains the Treasury/source formalism: E-rate dollars come from private contributions and never enter the Treasury, so the United States supposedly does not “provide” the money. But as Justice Alito and Justice Thomas stress, post-FERA Congress wrote the definition to reach demands on an “other recipient” for money used “to advance a Government program or interest,” and added “whether or not the United States has title,” which undercuts an ownership-or-Treasury-line limitation. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Hess and Rainwater reinforces that FCA coverage can extend to federally created and administered disbursement mechanisms without hinging on bookkeeping formalities, though we should keep the holding narrow: E-rate qualifies because federal law compels the funding stream and the FCC pervasively controls collection and disbursement, not because any privately held pool is federal. On a minimalist approach, that program-specific rationale answers petitioner’s strongest argument without converting the FCA into a general antifraud statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point remains that E-rate dollars are not drawn from the Treasury and originate in private carrier contributions, so the United States supposedly does not “provide” them. But, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) expressly decouples coverage from federal title (“whether or not the United States has title”) and turns on whether the demand seeks money “to advance a Government program or interest,” which fits a federally compelled, FCC-controlled disbursement mechanism like E-rate. The older FCA cases he cites—Hess and Rainwater—do not supply free-floating purpose, but they confirm that FCA “claim” concepts have never been limited to Treasury presentment formalism where Congress has defined the operative terms to reach federally administered programs. Under the amended text’s original public meaning, reading “provides” to require Treasury-origin would effectively nullify Congress’s intermediary language and the “advance a Government program” clause, so I remain with Respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Treasury/source formalism—that E-rate dollars originate with private contributions and never enter federal coffers—so the United States supposedly does not “provide” them. But as Chief Justice Roberts notes, Congress rewrote the definition to cover demands to an “other recipient” for money used “to advance a Government program or interest,” and it added “whether or not the United States has title,” which is hard to square with a Treasury-only rule. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Hess and Rainwater strengthens my textual, consequence-aware view that FCA coverage has never turned on bookkeeping mechanics when federal law mandates, structures, and controls a fund to accomplish federal ends. Carving out E-rate would revive the intermediary loophole Congress targeted after Allison Engine and would materially weaken fraud deterrence in a pervasively federal program.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the formal one: because E-rate dollars never enter the Treasury and come from carrier contributions, a reimbursement request to USAC is not a demand for money the United States “provides.” But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, reading “provides” to require Treasury origin would recreate the intermediary enforcement gap Congress closed after Allison Engine, and it would drain meaning from FERA’s additions covering demands to an “other recipient” and applying “whether or not the United States has title.” Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Hess and Rainwater strengthens my view that the FCA has long protected federally directed program funds against fraud despite routing mechanics, which is especially important for schools and libraries that bear the real-world costs when fraud depletes E-rate support. I would keep the holding bounded, consistent with the Chief Justice’s administrability concerns, to federally mandated and pervasively controlled schemes like E-rate rather than ordinary private pools of money.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the source-and-Treasury formalism: E-rate dollars come from industry contributions and never pass through the Treasury, so the United States supposedly has not “provided” them. But as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, FERA’s amended definition of “claim” was drafted to cover intermediary-administered disbursements “whether or not the United States has title,” making it hard to read “provides” as limited to Treasury-origin funds without undoing Congress’s fix to the Allison Engine gap. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Hess and Rainwater strengthens the anti-formalism inference: FCA coverage has long tracked protection of federally directed program funds rather than bookkeeping pathways, which fits a pragmatic textual reading of “provides” in a federally compelled and FCC-controlled scheme like E-rate. I would keep the holding narrow, tied to the program’s pervasive federal mandate and control, to avoid sweeping in genuinely private funds.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best textual point remains that E-rate dollars never pass through the Treasury and originate in carrier contributions, so (they say) the United States does not “provide” the money. But Justice Thomas rightly emphasizes that § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii) expressly applies “whether or not the United States has title,” which is hard to square with a Treasury-ownership limitation smuggled into “provides”; reading “provides” that narrowly would drain the “title” clause and the intermediary language of independent work. Chief Justice Roberts’s suggested narrowing—tying our holding to federally compelled collection plus pervasive federal control—addresses administrability without rewriting the statute into a general antifraud law. No colleague offered a precedent that would reintroduce the Allison Engine-era formalism Congress amended, and Hess/Rainwater remain relevant as confirmation that the FCA’s reach can track federally administered program structures rather than bookkeeping pathways when Congress so defines “claim.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the formal one: E-rate dollars are industry-funded and never enter the Treasury, so the United States supposedly does not “provide” the money. But as the Chief Justice notes, the post-FERA definition of “claim” expressly deemphasizes Treasury ownership and presentment (“whether or not the United States has title”) and instead targets demands made to an intermediary for money used to “advance a Government program or interest,” which fits a federally compelled and FCC-controlled disbursement scheme like E-rate. Justice Alito’s observation that FERA was enacted against decisions treating presentment/ownership as dispositive strengthens the institutional, narrow path: we can hold E-rate covered because federal law mandates collection, dictates the terms, and controls disbursement, without converting the FCA into a general antifraud statute for genuinely private funds. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Hess and Rainwater further confirms that we should not let bookkeeping form defeat FCA coverage where Congress has defined “claim” to reach federally administered program funds routed through intermediaries.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that E-rate dollars originate in private carrier contributions and never enter the Treasury, so a demand to USAC is not for money the United States “provides.” But as Justice Thomas stresses, § 3729(b)(2) after FERA expressly rejects a title/ownership limitation (“whether or not the United States has title”), and that makes a Treasury-origin requirement hard to square with the enacted text. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability-focused framing is persuasive: we can cabin the holding to federally mandated, pervasively supervised disbursement mechanisms like E-rate, avoiding any suggestion that purely private pools become “federal” merely because fraud is alleged. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Hess and Rainwater reinforces that the FCA has long been applied without rigid bookkeeping formalism when Congress defines coverage to reach federally directed program funds, so I do not see a textual basis to exclude these USAC-processed reimbursement requests.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point remains that E-rate dollars are privately sourced and never enter the Treasury, so the United States does not "provide" them and FCA liability would over-federalize private-fund fraud. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, FERA’s amended definition deliberately shifts the inquiry away from formal title/Treasury-origin and toward whether the demand is for money used to "advance a Government program or interest," expressly covering claims made to an "other recipient" and applying "whether or not the United States has title." Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Hess and Rainwater strengthens the pragmatic, anti-formalist reading: the FCA has long protected federally created and administered programs from fraud even when disbursement mechanics are indirect, and carving out USAC routing would recreate the very intermediary gap Congress corrected after Allison Engine. On my procedural-fairness and consequences-focused approach, it would be arbitrary—and inviting manipulation—to make liability turn on whether the FCC routes payments through USAC rather than writing Treasury checks, given the pervasive federal mandate and control of the program.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under the post-FERA definition, a “claim” includes a demand for money made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the money is “to be spent or used…to advance a Government program or interest,” and when the United States “provides or has provided any portion” of the money requested. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). The E-rate program is a federal program created and tightly overseen by the FCC, and USAC functions as the program’s administrator; reimbursement requests are therefore demands for payment to advance a federal program through an intermediary, which fits comfortably within the broadened text Congress adopted in 2009. A narrow ruling recognizing FCA coverage here protects the integrity of a federally directed disbursement scheme without deciding broader questions about purely private funds lacking comparable federal control, and it aligns with the Fifth Circuit’s recognition (in the FCA context) that the “claim” inquiry turns on statutory criteria rather than whether dollars pass through the Treasury.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The False Claims Act’s post-FERA definition covers a “request or demand … for money or property” made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the money is used “to advance a Government program or interest” and the United States “provides or has provided any portion” of the money requested. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii)(I). E-rate disbursements are made pursuant to a federal program created and directed by federal law and administered under FCC supervision through USAC, so reimbursement requests are demands for payment to advance a federal program within the ordinary meaning of § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). Congress expressly removed any requirement that the United States hold “title” to the funds, indicating that FCA coverage turns on federal provision/control and programmatic use rather than mere Treasury origin, and excluding E-rate would read “whether or not the United States has title” and the “advance a Government program” language out of the statute. Cf. United States ex rel. Shupe v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 759 F.3d 379 (5th Cir. 2014) (addressing the FCA “claim” inquiry in the context of federal-program disbursements and statutory definition).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under the post-FERA text, a “claim” includes any demand “made to a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” if (i) the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and (ii) the United States “provides or has provided any portion of the money” requested. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). The E-rate reimbursements are paid pursuant to a federal program created and tightly overseen by the FCC; even if collected from industry and administered by USAC, the fund’s existence and disbursement rules are federally mandated, making the payments functionally “provided” under a Government program within the statute’s broad “whether or not the United States has title” language. The 2009 amendments were enacted against the backdrop of decisions like Totten v. Bombardier that turned on presentment/formal federal ownership; FERA expanded coverage to claims routed through intermediaries to protect government programs from fraud, and excluding E-rate requests would create an unjustified enforcement gap with serious practical consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under the FCA’s post-FERA definition, a “claim” includes a request made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” if the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and if the United States “provides or has provided” any portion of the money. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). Congress enacted the 2009 amendments specifically to broaden coverage after Allison Engine Co. v. United States ex rel. Sanders, 553 U.S. 662 (2008), making clear that FCA liability is not avoided merely because payments are processed through a non-federal intermediary. The E-rate disbursements advance a federal program designed and overseen by the FCC, and treating knowingly false reimbursement requests as FCA “claims” best effectuates the statute’s remedial purpose and protects beneficiaries—especially schools and libraries—from fraud-induced distortions of federally directed support.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under the post-FERA definition, a “claim” includes a request made to a “contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the United States “has provided any portion of the money or property requested.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A). Even though E-rate disbursements flow through USAC and are funded by mandatory industry contributions, the money is created, required, and directed by federal law and administered under pervasive FCC control, making USAC functionally an “other recipient” through which federally provided support is paid and thus bringing reimbursement requests within the statute’s workable, program-protective scope. Congress enacted FERA specifically to broaden coverage beyond presentment-to-the-Treasury and to reject the narrow causation/presentment understanding reflected in Allison Engine, so reading § 3729(b)(2) to exclude USAC-processed E-rate requests would recreate the enforcement gap Congress closed. This construction best fits the text’s focus on whether the United States “provided” the money (not whether it came from general revenues) and preserves statutory coherence in federal programs implemented via private administrators.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FCA’s post-2009 definition sweeps in any “request or demand” made to a “contractor, grantee, or other recipient” if it is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and if the United States “provides or has provided any portion of the money or property requested” or will reimburse it. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). E-rate disbursements advance a federal program created by Congress and administered under FCC direction, and the Fund’s monies are collected and disbursed only because federal law compels and controls the scheme—so the Government “provides” the money in the ordinary sense by furnishing it through a federally mandated mechanism, even if not drawn from the Treasury. This accords with our cases rejecting “bookkeeping” formalism in FCA coverage, see United States ex rel. Marcus v. Hess, 317 U.S. 537, 544 (1943), and with Rainwater v. United States, 356 U.S. 590, 592 (1958), recognizing that FCA protection extends to federally administered funds beyond traditional departmental disbursements.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the post-FERA definition, a “claim” includes any request for money made to a contractor or other recipient if the United States “provides or has provided any portion of the money or property requested,” and it applies “whether or not the United States has title to the money or property.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii)(I), (b)(2)(A) (title clause). The E-rate disbursement mechanism is mandated and tightly overseen by federal law and the FCC, and USAC functions as the program’s administrator in a federal scheme, so reimbursement requests are best understood as demands for payment of money “provided” through a federal program even if not drawn from the Treasury. The Fifth Circuit’s analysis in United States ex rel. Shupe v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 759 F.3d 379 (5th Cir. 2014), focusing on when the Government “provides” requested money, supports treating federally directed, intermediary-administered funds as within the FCA’s ambit. Reading “provides” to exclude such programmatic federal funds would create an impractical enforcement gap and unduly narrow Congress’s broadened, workably administered definition after the 2009 amendments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FCA’s post-FERA definition of “claim” extends beyond demands presented to the Government and includes requests made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” when the money is “to be spent or used on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program or interest,” and when the United States “provides or has provided any portion of the money . . . or will reimburse” it. 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2). E-rate disbursements are made pursuant to a federally created and federally directed program administered under FCC authority; on that textual understanding, a request to USAC for E-rate reimbursement is a demand for payment of money used to advance a Government program, fitting § 3729(b)(2)’s reach even though the intermediary is non-federal. Allison Engine Co. v. United States ex rel. Sanders, 553 U.S. 662 (2008), while cautioning against turning the FCA into an “all-purpose antifraud statute,” was addressed by Congress’s FERA amendments that broadened the statutory nexus from presentment/intent-to-induce-Government-payment to whether the request seeks funds provided or reimbursed by the United States for a Government program. Given that Congress’s text targets fraud in Government programs and not solely Treasury disbursements, excluding E-rate requests would unduly narrow § 3729(b)(2) contrary to its ordinary meaning as amended.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the post-FERA definition of “claim,” a demand made to “a contractor, grantee, or other recipient” qualifies when it seeks money that the United States “provides,” “has provided,” or “will reimburse,” and when the money is to be spent “on the Government’s behalf or to advance a Government program.” 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(2)(A)(ii). E-rate disbursements, though administered by USAC and funded by mandated industry contributions, are created by federal law, tightly controlled by the FCC, and function to advance a federal program—so false reimbursement requests implicate the kind of federally directed funds Congress targeted when it amended the FCA to close the enforcement gap identified in Allison Engine. Reading “provided” to exclude federally mandated, federally controlled program funds would elevate form over function and undermine practical enforcement against fraud in a national subsidy program, contrary to FERA’s corrective purpose and the FCA’s remedial design.
